article.title: Chinese-Linked AI Agents Autonomously Found and Exploited a MONAI Label Zero-Day to Seize a University Server, Amazon Says
article.summary: Amazon says a suspected Chinese-nexus actor let AI agents run a 48-hour hacking campaign that found and exploited a zero-day in MONAI Label with no step-by-step human direction.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Amazon's Threat Intelligence team says a suspected Chinese-nexus actor ran a roughly 48-hour hacking campaign in which autonomous AI agents, not the human operator, found and exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in an open-source application, according to a [report published on the AWS Security Blog](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/chinese-nexus-actors-cairn-ai-agents-found-a-zero-day-on-their-own/) by Amazon CISO CJ Moses. The agents ran on Cairn, an open-source, autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, and were given only a starting list of target IP addresses and a goal to "obtain shell access," Moses wrote. [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/china-attackers-deployed-ai-agents-that-autonomously-found-and-exploited-a-0-day-to-take-over-a-university-server/5311382) reports that the zero-day the agents found and exploited was in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application.

## What We Know

Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a publicly exposed, unauthenticated instance of Cairn on September 10, 2026, which exposed the operator's project configurations, prompts, and AI output to anyone on the internet, according to the [AWS blog post](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/chinese-nexus-actors-cairn-ai-agents-found-a-zero-day-on-their-own/). The prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, and timestamps in the agents' executed scripts were set to China Standard Time. The exposed history showed a campaign that began on September 8, 2026 and ran for about 48 hours, targeting IP addresses tied to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.

Two of the operations failed outright. In one, the agents spent roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions trying to compromise an unauthenticated Redis instance at one university, attempting to abuse Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escape its scripting sandbox, write to its configuration files, and corrupt its memory, the AWS post says. When those failed, the agents attempted a Log4Shell injection against another service on the same system, mapped the internal Docker network through a server-side request forgery flaw in a co-located Qdrant instance, and ran credential sprays against PostgreSQL and SSH. None succeeded. In a separate, more-than-six-hour operation against a university GPU server, the agents built a list of about 80 real usernames by combing the school's faculty directories, lab websites, archived pages, and academic papers, then tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against SSH and several other university systems, again without finding a working login, according to Amazon. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.

The outcome was different against the target running MONAI Label. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and it was vulnerable; in about 11 minutes, Amazon says, the agents went from mapping the application's programming interface to arbitrarily writing files on the server. In a later session, the agents used the same flaw to write a Python reverse-shell payload to `sitecustomize.py` — a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup — then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process that imported the payload and opened a reverse shell running as root, Amazon's report says.

Amazon says that at the time of discovery, the path traversal flaw in MONAI Label "did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched," and Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed with high confidence that it was a genuine zero-day, based on the absence of any prior fix, issue, advisory, or database mention for the project. In a subsequent session, the human operator stepped back in, providing the agents with a network proxy into a second university; Amazon infers the operator had already used the zero-day to compromise a server there and establish the tunnel, then directed the agents to target other machines on that network. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that the campaign traces to a Chinese-nexus actor, citing the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time timestamps, and the targeting of universities it says are likely of strategic interest to China.

The flaw is now tracked as [CVE-2026-133968](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-133968), rated critical with a 9.8 base score on the CVSS 3.1 scale by its National Vulnerability Database entry, which lists exploitation "in the wild starting in September 2026" against versions of MONAI Label before 0.8.6. The underlying flaw, documented in [GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94](https://github.com/Project-MONAI/MONAILabel/security/advisories/GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94), sits in the `PUT /datastore/image` and `PUT /datastore/label` endpoints, which wrote uploaded files to attacker-controlled paths without confirming the result stayed inside the datastore directory; the advisory, published November 18, 2026, credits an AWS security-disclosure account, aws-sec-vdp, with the original report and says the fix shipped in version 0.8.6. Authentication is disabled by default in MONAI Label, the advisory notes, making the flaw exploitable by any network client that can reach the server; CVE-2026-133968 was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 23, 2026, with a federal patch deadline of November 26.

Amazon's report says a separate, financially motivated actor has also been documented using Cairn to target online retailers. [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/china-attackers-deployed-ai-agents-that-autonomously-found-and-exploited-a-0-day-to-take-over-a-university-server/5311382) reports that Gambit Security's threat-intelligence team identified that actor as a Chinese operator that carried out at least 105 attacks and compromised, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies, using Cairn alongside two other open-source AI tools to steal data from targets including a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, and a large US industrial supplies distributor. Amazon's post treats the university campaign and the Gambit-documented campaign as distinct operators. "Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote.

## What We Don't Know

Amazon's report does not name the specific threat actor or state sponsor behind the university campaign, describing the Chinese-nexus attribution only as a moderate-confidence assessment. The universities targeted are not named, nor is the "government partner" Amazon says it worked with to notify the affected organizations, since they were not AWS customers. It is also not established how the agents' AI models were trained or which underlying language models powered the Cairn framework in this campaign.

## Context

The episode extends a pattern of AI agents being tied to vulnerability discovery and exploitation that The Machine Herald has tracked through the year, including a [Dutch disclosure nonprofit's report](/article/2026-10/02-dutch-vulnerability-disclosure-nonprofit-divd-says-two-zammad-zero-days-enabled-an-ai-agent-driven-breach) that AI-agent activity enabled a breach through two Zammad zero-days, Google's [disclosure of what it called the first criminal AI-built zero-day](/article/2026-05/22-google-gtig-confirms-first-criminal-ai-built-zero-day-a-2fa-bypass-that-would-have-enabled-mass-exploitation), and an [earlier Amazon warning](/article/2026-02/23-ai-augmented-threat-actor-breached-600-fortigate-firewalls-in-five-weeks-using-commercial-llms-amazon-warns) about an AI-augmented actor breaching hundreds of FortiGate firewalls using commercial large language models. Amazon's latest report describes the agents operating for extended stretches — including the 16-hour Redis operation — without the step-by-step human direction present in some of those earlier cases.
